newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICAN ACCIDENT FUND PROPOSALS AMENDED AGAIN.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICAN ACCIDENT FUND PROPOSALS AMENDED AGAIN.

text.p: The government has revised its controversial policy paper on reforms to the Road Accident Fund to reduce claims and thereby the escalating cost of South Africa's high accident rate.

Releasing the third draft of the "white paper" on Wednesday, Transport Minister Mac Maharaj said that he hoped the new policy on the fund -- previously known as the Multilateral Motor Vehicle Accidents Fund (MMF) -- would be finalised by September, with new legislation in place early next year.
South Africa has one of the highest road accident rates in the world, with 517,669 recorded last year of which 84,173 resulted in serious injuries including 10,000 deaths.

Over the last few years it has been paying out ever increasing amounts to the injured and families of the dead. In 1996 payments totalled 1.3 billion rand while the fund's deficit rose to 6.3 billion rand by April 1996 and was expected to have increased to eight billion rand by April this year.
Transport Director-General Khetso Gordhan said the long time taken to process and settle claims hid the real nature of the problem and it was obvious that the system had to be changed.

Because the fund had received some exorbitant claims, it had been decided to limit the maximum payouts to between 1.2 and 1.3 million rand. The fund had already settled claims of between 15 and 16 million rand.
Claims would only be paid to people earning an after-tax income of up to 4,000 rand with anyone earning above that expected to insure themselves.
"That will cover 80 to 85 percent of income earners," Gordhan said.
All victims, regardless of fault, would have immediate access to emergency and acute medical treatment while permanent impairment and death benefits would be calculated on a fault basis.

Because of the long delays experienced in having claims settled in court, with resultant high legal costs that took up most of the money paid out, a special tribunal would be established to judge claims.

Gordhan admitted that one of the most controversial provisions that had been maintained was the abrogation of common law rights that did not allow victims to sue those who caused the accident as well as claim from the fund.
This would prevent cases where drivers had been stripped of all their possessions, even if they were low-income earners.
He admitted that this could be challenged in the Constitutional Court but past experience had shown that such cases would not be supported by the court.
Gordhan denied that this clause was "anti-lawyers" , who took the bulk of the amounts settled each year to pay for the costs of claims.

The fund is financed by a levy on petrol and Maharaj said it had been argued that the deficit could be wiped out by increasing the levy by anything up to 65 cents a litre compared to the present 17.3 cents.
This, however, went against government's pledge not to increase the overall tax burden and he would rather see smaller increases a little above the inflation rate each year while limiting payouts.
Because the root of the problem lay in the country's high accident rate, Maharaj said that the fund would be investing about 37.5 million rand a year in road management and road safety.
"We will want to see a return for our money," he said.
